prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayers at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, founding moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single B006 prize to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer. The reasoning has been sharpened by round 1. What the committee would honour is two secure things: the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, which predicted that interlayer tunnelling flattens the bands near a small twist angle, and the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle. Neither depends on solving the pairing problem. Eriksson put it well: the single-particle flat band is quantitatively tested, while the many-body states built on it are not yet understood, and I agree the citation must say exactly that and nothing more. The field that followed (moire transition-metal dichalcogenides, fractional Chern insulators, twist-controlled devices) shows the idea is general and not a single-sample curiosity, which is the property I weigh most: a simple mechanism that carries over to other materials.
statement.case_against: I accept the force of the objections raised against my own choice. The pairing mechanism is unsettled, sample-to-sample and twist-angle variation is large, and the three-name limit leaves out Yuan Cao, who was first author of the 2018 papers, and independent groups (Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov and others). Bistritzer's share relative to other flat-band theorists is a judgement I cannot fully verify here. Against all this, B015 is the better-attributed candidate: eight of eight members ranked it, all proposed the same two names, and its results are reproduced at the 1e-18 level in several laboratories. If the committee decides that the unresolved interpretation and the Cao question weigh more than the secure prediction and discovery, B015 is a legitimate prize and I would not regard it as a poor outcome.

responses.point: Kroll argues that a field with an unresolved central mechanism is harder to describe in a short citation than a measurement that works, and that topological insulators, my second choice, bring the question of what they add beyond 2016 and the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang.
responses.response: The citation problem is real, but I think it is solvable by wording. A citation naming the flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated and superconducting states makes no claim about pairing, so it does not need the mechanism to be settled. On B055 I agree and have moved it down in practice: the 2016 prize and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission make it a weaker place for the three names than B006, which is why I keep it only as a second alternative. Your characterisation of the lattice clock as an original idea followed by a precision realization is one I share, which is why B015 is my first alternative.

responses.point: Lindroth defends the lattice clock as understood at a deep level, with systematic shifts modelled and cross-checked between laboratories, and says it tests gravitational redshift and constancy of constants, so it is not less fundamental, while agreeing that three names for B006 leave an uncomfortable theory-credit question.
responses.response: I accept the correction. The clock is understood in the way precision metrology is understood, through modelled and intercompared systematics, and that is a high standard I should not have implied was lower than a mechanism-based one. We do differ on what is the new idea: for me the magic-angle prediction is a mechanism that predicts where to look and was then found there, whereas the clock is an invention that is then perfected. On your credit worry I agree it is the weakest part of B006. Since the committee cannot add Cao, I would defend the theory pair of Bistritzer and MacDonald as the origin of the prediction, with Jarillo-Herrero standing for the experimental discovery, and say openly that the third name is the most contestable.

responses.point: Eriksson says the flat band is well understood and tested but the emergent many-body states and superconducting pairing are contested, so the citation should stay anchored on the flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated states.
responses.response: I agree and I have rewritten the citation along those lines: it now names the prediction of flat bands at a magic angle and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, and avoids any phrase implying a theory of the superconductivity. You are also right that I overstated 'understood' in round 1. The flat band is understood; the phases it hosts are observed and only partly explained. I keep my view that waiting for the pairing question to close is not a good criterion, because for a field that is still moving it may not close for a long time, and the attribution does not become simpler with time.

responses.point: Olsson finds the theory-then-experiment sequence persuasive but would want a few more years of settled mechanism, notes that Yuan Cao is outside the credited names, and says she would not stand in the way if the discovery is judged secure apart from its interpretation.
responses.response: That last condition is exactly my claim, and I am glad it is acceptable to you: the existence of the correlated phases and the flat band is not disputed by anyone in this exchange, and the chair's summary records that as agreed. On the timing, I think a decade of settled mechanism is a standard we do not apply to most prize-winning discoveries at the moment of award. The Cao point I cannot answer by argument, only by saying that it is a limit of the three-person rule and not a flaw in the science, and that the citation should be honest about it.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube as a clue from nature and a bold instrument that opened a new messenger, and says the Halzen, Karle and Spiering trio is imperfect but workable.
responses.response: I agree that IceCube opened a real window and I regard the diffuse flux as solid. My difficulty is in distinguishing the three names from a collaboration of hundreds and from the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage, which you concede is imperfect, and Olsson's two-name version differs again. With the allocation unsettled I would not rank B007 above B006 or B015 in this cycle, though I think it is a strong candidate for a later year when the names and the source populations are better settled by KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the unsettled superconducting pairing and the sample variability as a reason to defer, or the flat-band prediction plus the experimental discovery as sufficient now.

Whether Bistritzer is the right third name beside MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, and how to handle Yuan Cao and the independent groups within a three-person limit; my recollection of the early priority history is not verified against sources here.

How far the five-member preference for B015 and its clean two-name attribution should count against my judgement that B006 is the stronger scientific case; I do not treat the count as a substitute for the science, but I recognise that the attribution argument is a scientific one too.
Whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes make B015 an increment, a point on which I defer to the atomic physicists, and whether the 2016 prize reduces the appetite for B055.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have no known collaboration with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer or with any credited candidate on this shortlist. I am a theorist in the same broad community as the flat-band work without direct ties, and I share a Gothenburg environment with colleagues Johansson and Olsson, which bears only on B024 and B013 and not on my preferred configuration.
